input: It has been determined that the reboiler wall thickness is 35 mm once the corrosion allowance has been added, and it is important to appreciate what this figure actually represents. In essence, the pressure case establishes the thickness of metal that the wall requires in order to contain the design pressure safely, the corrosion allowance is then added on top of that requirement, and the resulting total is the 35 mm wall that the fabricator will be asked to produce. It should be emphasised that this thickness is not a $\Delta P$ allowance, and no portion of it is available to be traded away against pressure drop elsewhere in the circuit, since a thinner wall obtained by eroding the allowance would simply consume the corrosion provision for a purpose it was never intended to serve. Attention now turns to the choice of gasket material for the reboiler flanges, which is to be made on the basis of temperature limit alone. Two candidate materials are currently under consideration, and the comparison between them has deliberately been kept narrow in scope: pressure rating, chemical resistance and cost are not in dispute between the pair, as both materials satisfy the duty in those respects and differ primarily in the respect that matters here. On this basis, the higher-rated material is preferred. The reboiler experiences the highest metal temperatures in this part of the unit, and the gasket is a component whose failure would arrive without the kind of warning signs that operators are able to act upon in good time. The lower-rated material would undoubtedly perform adequately at the normal operating temperature, and the argument in its favour rests squarely on that normal case, but the argument against it rests on the excursion case, in which temperatures climb beyond the normal band during disturbances of the kind the unit is known to experience, leaving a gasket that is already at its limit with no reserve whatsoever in hand.
target:
The reboiler wall thickness is 35 mm after the corrosion allowance is added. The figure is a pressure-boundary thickness: the pressure case sets the metal the wall needs, the corrosion allowance is added to that metal, and the sum is the 35 mm wall the fabricator is asked to roll. It is not a $\Delta P$ allowance, and no part of it is available to be traded against pressure drop elsewhere in the circuit. A thinner wall bought back from the allowance would spend the corrosion provision on a duty it was not sized for.

The gasket choice at the reboiler flanges is made on temperature limit alone. Two candidate materials are in contention, and the comparison between them is deliberately narrow: pressure rating, chemical resistance and cost are not in dispute between the pair, because both meet the duty on those counts and differ where it matters here. The higher-rated material takes the preference. The reboiler sees the highest metal temperatures in this part of the unit, and the gasket is the component whose failure arrives without warning signs the operators can act on. A gasket at its temperature limit does not degrade on a schedule the inspection round can follow; it holds until it does not. The lower-rated material would serve at the normal operating temperature, and the argument for it rests on that normal case. The argument against it rests on the excursion case, where the temperature climbs past the normal band during the disturbances the unit is known to see, and where a gasket already at its limit has nothing in reserve. On temperature limit alone, the material with the reserve is the defensible choice, and that margin, not any wider merit, is the whole of the reason for the preference.
